property_summary: For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether, the contract preserves that caller's guess slot until they later settle (i.e., a subsequent lockInGuess from the same caller must be rejected); the mutant removes this uniqueness guard allowing the same caller to overwrite an existing locked guess, which the reference forbids.

After lockInGuess returns, the stored guess.block must be strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was called (i.e., reference stores block.number+1); the mutant storing block.number violates this because it records a block equal to the current block.

After a successful lockInGuess call, the stored Guess.block for the caller is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was executed (reference stores block.number+1, mutant stores block.number and thus can violate this), so the rule is: for any caller and guess, lockInGuess must return a stored block > the block at call-time; the mutant can break this by storing block.number.

After a successful lockInGuess call, the stored Guess.block for the caller must be strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was executed; the mutant that writes block.number (not block.number+1) can store a block equal to the call-time block and thus violate this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and guess value, after calling lockInGuess with the required 1 ether, the stored guesses(caller).block must be nonzero and strictly greater than the block number at which the call to lockInGuess was made; the mutant that stores block.number (instead of block.number+1) can make the stored block equal to the call-time block for some inputs, violating this rule.

For any caller and guess, after successfully calling lockInGuess with 1 ether the stored guesses(caller).block must be strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was executed; the mutant that stores block.number (not block.number+1) can store an equal block and thus violate this rule for some inputs.

After a successful lockInGuess call by any address sending 1 ether, the stored guess for that address (guesses(address).guess) is nonzero immediately after the call in the reference contract; the mutant that writes the block before the guess can leave the stored guess observable as zero during call execution (and thus lead to a different visible value immediately after), so for some fuzzed caller the mutant will violate this property.

For any caller who sends exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, immediately after the call the stored guess for that caller (guesses(caller).guess) is nonzero in the correct contract; the mutant that sets block before guess can make the stored guess observable as zero for some caller and thus violate this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract ALWAYS stores the provided guess value (non-zero iff the fuzzed bytes32 is non-zero) observable immediately after the call via the auto-generated public getter; the mutant that assigns block before guess can cause the stored guess to be observed as zero for some caller, violating this invariant.

For any caller sending exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, immediately after the call the stored guess returned by the public getter equals the bytes32 value they provided; the mutant that sets block before guess can make the stored getter return zero for some fuzzed caller/input and thus violate this rule.

After any successful lockInGuess call (caller sends exactly 1 ether), the public getter for guesses(caller).block is nonzero and strictly greater than block.number (i.e., it stores block.number+1); the mutant that swaps assignments can briefly set block before guess causing observable inconsistent state for some interleaving and thus can violate the expected stored block value for some fuzzed caller/inputs.

For any caller and guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call the contract's stored guess for that caller equals the hash just provided; the mutant that writes a zero to guesses[msg.sender].guess before setting the hash can be observed to have performed a visible intermediate write (causing an extra SSTORE) which can change the return/gas/observable behavior for some inputs — specifically a fuzzed caller and hash can reveal a difference in whether a direct call to lockInGuess returns (succeeds) or not when trying to re-lock (the reference enforces require(guesses[msg.sender].block==0) and leaves guess equal to the hash, while the mutant's extra write can make the storage behavior differ in ways the fuzzer can detect by calling lockInGuess twice and checking the second call's success), so the rule is: for any caller and hash, the first lockInGuess call should succeed (return without revert) and subsequent lockInGuess by same caller should revert; the mutant can break this for some inputs.

For any caller and guess hash, the first call to lockInGuess should succeed (not revert) and store the provided guess such that a public read of guesses[caller].guess equals the provided hash immediately after; the mutant that writes zero before setting the hash causes an observable intermediate state that can make the stored guess readable as zero in some cases (e.g., due to how the getter is synthesized for the struct's field ordering), so for some fuzzed caller/hash the mutant will make the public getter return zero while the reference always returns the provided hash.

For any caller and guess hash, the first call to lockInGuess with 1 ether must succeed (not revert) and leave the contract such that a subsequent call to lockInGuess by the same caller will revert because guesses[caller].block is non-zero; the mutant's extra intermediate write changes storage/write ordering causing some sequences (same caller, same hash) to make the second call unexpectedly succeed or behave differently, violating this rule.

For any caller and guess hash, calling lockInGuess(bytes32) with exactly 1 ether always returns (does not revert) and leaves guesses[caller].block != 0 immediately after the call; the mutant's extra intermediate write can change storage semantics so for some caller/hash the call still returns but guesses[caller].block can be observed as 0 (due to altered storage interaction), violating the rule.

For any caller and guess hash, the first call to lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always succeeds (does not revert) and leaves the stored guess for that caller (the public getter guesses(caller).guess) equal to the provided hash; the mutant that writes zero to guesses[msg.sender].guess before setting the hash can cause a differing visible stored value for some fuzzed caller/hash, violating this rule.

For any player who locks in a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference C pays out 2 ether if and only if their stored guess equals the computed answer; the mutant inverts that condition and will pay when the guess does NOT equal the answer (so the general rule: settle only pays when guess == answer — the mutant violates this for inputs where guess == answer).

After a successful settle call the contract's balance decreases iff the stored guess did not match the computed blockhash-derived answer — the correct contract only transfers (reduces balance) when guess == answer, whereas the mutant inverts that and may transfer when guess == answer, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any player that locked a guess and later calls settle after the chosen block, the reference contract only transfers 2 ether when the stored guess equals the computed blockhash-derived answer; the mutant inverts this and thus can transfer 2 ether when the stored guess equals the answer (violating that the transfer condition is equality).

After a caller locks a guess for a future block and that block is mined, calling settle only transfers 2 ether when the stored guess equals the computed answer; the mutant inverts that condition and will transfer when the guess does NOT equal the answer, so there exists a fuzzed guess value that causes a differing transfer outcome.

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle after the target block never reduces the contract balance unless the stored guess equals the computed answer; the mutant inverts the equality and can reduce the balance for inputs where the stored guess equals the answer.

For any caller who had locked a guess, after calling settle the reference contract always clears their stored guess record (block == 0) regardless of whether the guess matched; the mutant only clears the record when the guess matches, so for some inputs (a losing guess) the stored block remains non-zero.

For any caller that locked a guess and then calls settle, the reference contract always resets their stored guess.block to 0 after settle returns; the mutant leaves guess.block nonzero when the guess was incorrect (so the property is violated for some inputs).

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle in the same block as the stored block must revert (reference requires block.number > storedBlock); the mutant allowing block.number >= storedBlock lets settle succeed (or proceed) in the same block, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any account that has locked a guess, the reference contract always reverts if settle() is called in the SAME block as the stored guess block (requires block.number > storedBlock), whereas the mutant allowing block.number >= storedBlock lets settle() proceed in that same-block case and thus not revert.

Reference C never allows settle() to succeed in the exact block when a guess was locked (it requires block.number > storedBlock), so for any address that locked a guess, calling settle() in the same block must revert; the mutant that changes the check to >= can let settle() proceed (not revert) for those same-block calls, violating this rule.

For any address that has locked a guess, calling settle() in the same block as the stored guess block always reverts on the correct contract (block.number must be strictly greater than stored block); the mutant that allows >= lets settle proceed (succeed or not revert) for some inputs — detect by observing whether settle() succeeds when invoked in the same block as lockInGuess was called.

For any address that has locked a guess, calling settle() in the same block as lockInGuess must always revert on the correct contract (it requires block.number > storedBlock); the mutant that weakens the check to >= can allow settle() to proceed (not revert) in that same-block situation for some inputs.

For any caller who previously locked a guess with block = k, calling settle after block > k never causes the contract balance to increase (i.e., the contract either pays out 2 ether to the caller only if their stored guess equals keccak256(blockhash(k))); the mutant that replaces keccak256(blockhash(k)) with bytes32(uint256(k)) can be guessed deterministically and thus can cause a payout for guesses that wouldn't match the real blockhash-derived answer, breaking the invariant relating payouts to blockhash-derived answers (observable via address(c).balance).

For any caller and any stored guess-block pair, when settle() is called after the stored block, the correct contract never treats the stored block number itself as the answer (i.e., the payout condition only depends on keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock))), whereas the mutant treats bytes32(uint256(storedBlock)) as the answer and therefore can pay out for guesses equal to that deterministic conversion — so the invariant is: after lockInGuess(...) then advancing to block > storedBlock and calling settle(), the returned answer (as observable via whether settle pays out) can only be true if the caller's guess equals keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)) — the mutant violates this because bytes32(uint256(storedBlock)) can equal the stored guess even when keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)) does not.

For any locked guess, after advancing to a later block and calling settle(), the correct contract only pays out when the stored guess equals keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)); the mutant instead treats bytes32(uint256(storedBlock)) as the answer so there exist inputs (a guessed value equal to bytes32(storedBlock) but not equal to keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock))) that make the mutant pay out while the reference never does.

For any actor and block chosen when locking a guess, the reference contract only pays out in settle() if the stored guess equals keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock)); the mutant instead treats bytes32(uint256(storedBlock)) as the answer, so there exist fuzzed inputs (actor + guess + warp/roll to advance block) where the mutant will pay out but the reference never does.

For any address that locked a guess and after advancing to a later block, the reference contract never treats the stored block number itself as the correct answer (payout only occurs if guess == keccak256(blockhash(storedBlock))), whereas the mutant uses bytes32(uint256(storedBlock)) as the answer, so there exist fuzzed inputs (guessed value equal to bytes32(storedBlock)) that cause the mutant to pay out but the reference never does.
